lines.text: The hall swallows the sound of your boots. Somebody has been waiting for you.
A dark robe, walking into the Adventure Society off the square. Nobody minds the colour so long as you can hold a line.
Contracts are on the boards behind me. Iron first — everyone starts on iron.
Back again. The boards have not moved since you last looked at them.
Ask, then. It is quicker than watching you decide.
Vail. I keep the boards honest and the floor swept. Both are harder than they sound.
Somebody wants something fought. You take the board's word for it and go and fight it.
Iron pays little and forgives much. Gold does neither.
Five floors. This one is registration, and it is open to anybody who can find the door.
Iron above us, then bronze, then silver, then gold. The stair knows what you are. Bel stands at the foot of it in case the stair is not persuasive enough.
The higher you go the emptier the boards get. There are three gold contracts in the province and two of them have been up for a year.

choices.say: How do I get to iron?

lines.text: You join by proving you will still be alive at the end of your first contract. We stopped taking people's word for it.
One room, one monster, one knife. Brann has the knife. The monster is an earth elemental and it is a weak one, which is not the same as an easy one.
It mends itself off bare earth. The floor of that room is half stone and half dirt, and that is the whole of the lesson.
You come back here with a headache and a bill from the healer. Then you go again.
Nobody has died in the proving room in eleven years. That is not luck, that is the room. It is also four people standing behind a grille you cannot see, being paid to be bored.
Down the passage, then. Keep it off the dirt, or keep it too busy to reach any.
You are standing there dripping, so I take it the elemental is gravel. Good. Sit down before you fall down.
Now the part that decides what you become. Three essences. Whatever those three come to between them is the fourth, and nobody chooses that one — it chooses itself.
Three. Take your time, and do not take fire because it is loud.
Signed, sealed and iron rank. The second floor is open to you, and Bel will stop looking at you like that.
Take something small first. The board up there is never empty and it forgives a great deal.
And here. Registration fee, returned — the Society charges it and then gives it back, which is the sort of thing the Society does. Spend it on the square before you take anything.

choices.say: How do I use any of this?
How does the Society count what I do?
What is on the higher floors?

lines.text: New Adventures. Nothing pinned to it yet. It goes up before the work does.

choices.say: I'll keep an eye on it.

lines.text: Read away. They do not bite, and neither do I. Mostly.
The register is here when you want it. The stair is there when you have earned it.
Proving knife. Society property. It comes back or you pay for it.
It is not a good knife. A good knife would teach you the wrong lesson.
Elementals of that sort do not chase well and do not think at all. Stand on the stone. Make it come to you across the stone.
If it gets a foot in the dirt it starts putting itself back together faster than you are taking it apart. Then you have a long afternoon.
Mind the step on the way down. It has had three of you this month.
Hold it. Iron rank up those stairs, and you are not on the roll yet.
Vail is at the desk behind you. Get signed, get proved, come back, and I will not say a word.
Not that floor. Bronze above us, and you are iron.
Close a few off this board and the stair will let you by. It is not personal. It is a ledger.
Silver, that. Bronze is as far as you go today.
The Society counts what you finish, not what you attempt. So finish more, and do try to be dull about it.
Gold floor. I am going to have to ask you to come back down.
There are three contracts up there. The Chapter reads out the name of everyone who goes up to look at them, and I have heard that list read at funerals.
Iron floor. Eighteen on the board this morning and there will be eighteen tomorrow. They are not the same eighteen and nobody minds which you take.
Name at the bottom, date at the top, and the sheet comes back to me either way. Especially the ones that went wrong.

choices.say: Does any of this get me to bronze?

lines.text: Bronze. Congratulations, the Society stops underwriting you here. If a bronze contract goes wrong it now goes wrong at your expense.
Board is still full, mind. There is more of this than there are people daft enough to do it.
Silver. Eight on the board, which is four more than I like.
Every one of them started as a bronze contract somebody did not come back from. That is what makes them silver. Not the danger. The precedent.

choices.say: How do I read one properly?
You have been up here a long time.

lines.text: Gold. Five. It is usually two.
I am obliged to say this part out loud, so: taking one of these is not accepting a contract. It is a decision about the rest of your life. There. Said.

choices.say: Do you have to say that to everyone?
I only came up to look.

lines.text: A walled floor, half laid in flagstone and half left as bare earth. The door behind you is not a door any more.
Something in the far corner is already getting up. It comes apart where the knife goes in, and it puts itself back together anywhere its feet find soil.
Keep it on the stone.
A stone about the size of a plum, and it stops being a stone the moment you swallow it. After that it is part of how you are put together.
Fire does not make you good at fire. It makes fire one of the things you are made of, and then your body works out what to do about that.
One ability from each to begin. The rest come later, out of stones the Society does not hand out and does not ask where you got.
Confluence. Three essences sit together long enough and they agree on something none of them said.
Some threes the registry knows by name. Some it does not, and then you write it up yourself and the Chapter files it under your name whether you wanted that or not.
It cannot be traded, refused or swapped. This is the one door in the building that only opens the once.

choices.say: That is a lot to sign for.

lines.text: Reach for it the way you reach for a pocket. It is in there now; it does not need words.
Right hand on the world opens what you can do with it — talk, trade, or cast. One to four if your hands are quicker than the menu, which in a fight they had better be.
Four of them, and each one comes out looking like whatever it is made of. You will know which is which the first time you throw one.

choices.say: And how does the Society count what I do?

lines.text: Mana. You have a shallow well of it and it fills back up on its own, slower than you will want.
Iron adventurers die with a full well more often than an empty one. Spend it.
That the tool did it. Give a man a good blade for his first fight and he spends nine years thinking he won that one.
This one is honest. If the thing falls over, that was you.
Knife.
It is a bit blunter than it was.
It was blunt when I gave it to you. You have chipped it, which is different, and which I am writing down.
Go on. Vail wants you at the desk before she loses the paperwork on purpose.
Rope. Twice as much rope as you think. Then a lamp, then something to eat that is not going to go off in a bag.
Everybody buys a sword. Nobody buys rope. Then a contract goes down a hole and I get a form to fill in.
There she is. On the roll, iron rank, and no longer my problem.
Second floor. Take the stair slowly the first time — it is taller than it looks from down here and it does the walking for you.
Silver, when I was worth something. Then a contract in the Hollows went the way those go.
Now I stand at the bottom of a staircase and tell people what they are. It is warm and nobody bleeds on me.
That does not sound like nothing.
No. It does not, does it.

choices.say: I will come back down and tell you how it went.

lines.text: Up you go. Boards do not read themselves, more is the pity.
The one you can walk to before dark. Not the one that pays.
Everybody takes the one that pays. I have a drawer of sheets from people who took the one that pays.
The road. Not the work — the road. Four hours out, four hours back, and the thing you were sent for takes ten minutes.
It is tired that gets you. Take water. Take a second pair of socks. I am entirely serious about the socks.
Good. Come back and tell me it was boring. Boring is my favourite word.
Iron, the Society covers your healer and your funeral. It is cheap for them and it keeps the intake up.
Bronze, you carry it. Read the fee, then read what it would cost you to be wrong, and take the difference seriously.
Nine years on this floor. I have stamped the sheet of everybody who ever got to silver out of this chapter.
Eleven of them. I could tell you all their names. I would rather tell you about the socks, honestly, but Ostrey has that one.
Go on. And sign it yourself — I am not forging another one.
Twice. Once for what it says and once for what it does not.
The clients are not lying to you. They are telling you the part they understand, and the part they do not understand is the part that is going to be waiting for you.
When a sheet is short, ask why it is short.

choices.say: You have been up here a long time.

lines.text: I keep the sheets of the ones that came back as well. People only ever ask about the others.
How many is that?
More. It is always more. Nobody believes me and I stopped minding about a decade ago.
Take your time on the stair. Nobody up here is in a hurry any more.
Two have been on that board for a year and the province has arranged itself around them. The other three went up this season, which is the part that is keeping me here late.
The third went up in the spring. I would rather it had not.

choices.say: Do you have to say that to everyone?

lines.text: To everyone who reaches this floor, yes. It is nine words in the charter and I have said them four times in eleven years.
Twice to the same man. He is the reason it is nine words and not four.
The stair is behind you. Nothing up here is going anywhere.
Stars. Four to a rank. You get them for closing contracts, and a contract that nearly killed you counts for more than one that did not.
Four stars at iron and the Society will hear an application for bronze. It is not automatic. Somebody reads the file.
Who reads it?
I do. So bring the sheets back, and write on them like a person and not like somebody hiding something.
You carry a copy. Everyone does — rank, stars, what you took and what it gave you.
The Society keeps the other one, and ours has more in it than yours does. That is not a threat, it is a filing system.
Four stars, and then Vail decides. Every sheet you bring back is a line on the file.
The ones that go wrong are lines too, mind. Better lines, sometimes. A person who came back and wrote down exactly how it went is worth two who came back and said it was fine.
Four stars. I have read the file, which is more than the Chapter does, and the file says you come back and you write it down.
So. Hold still.
She takes the seal out of the drawer, breathes on it, and presses it into the wax at the bottom of your sheet without any ceremony whatsoever.
There is a ceremony. It is in the spring and it is four hours long and half the people in it are dead by the following one.
This is the part that matters. The stair will let you up, and the floor above will let you take work that can kill you at your own expense.
Go up. Read twice. Come back down and tell me it was boring.
You have got the Society’s look about you. New, and holding nothing.
They took the knife back.
They always do. It is theirs. Everything on this side of the counter is not, and that is the whole difference between us.
Take your time. Nothing here will do you any good if you cannot hold it up at the end of an hour.
A dagger, first, because it is quick and it is cheap and you will not be sorry you spent the marks.
The spear when you can afford it. It reaches a thing before the thing reaches you, which at iron rank is most of the job.
And the axe when you have stopped missing. It is slow. If you miss with it you have simply given something four seconds.
Come back with marks and I will be delighted to see you.
Mind the shelf. Half of what is on it is worth more than you are and the other half will take your eyebrows off.
You want the red bottles. Everybody wants the red bottles.

choices.say: What do the red bottles do?

lines.text: They close what is open. That is all. They do not mend what is broken underneath it and they do not make you braver.
Carry one in your off hand and drink it while the thing is still swinging. A potion in your bag is a potion you did not drink.
Go on then. Do not shake them.
You will be back. They always are, and usually bleeding.
Rope, lamp oil, salt, boots. And one thing you cannot afford, which is why you came in.
A grey lump that is warm on one side. You hold it, it goes somewhere, and something you were always able to do you can suddenly do.
Which something?
That is the part nobody likes. It is not yours to pick. Five from each of your four and no more, and the order is the stone’s business.
They come out of monsters, mostly. Which is convenient, because the price of one in here is not a price so much as a discouragement.

choices.say: I will find my own, then.

lines.text: Everything has a price on it. The stones have two, and the second one is your patience.
Mind the step on your way out. Everyone forgets the step.
Three doors on the square, and you will want all of them eventually.
Sella at the Weaponry, on your left going out. Buy a dagger today. Bare hands are a thing people write about afterwards, not a thing people survive.
Ivens the apothecary opposite her, for the red bottles. Carry one in your off hand and drink it while the thing is still swinging.
And Corvel further up, who sells awakening stones at a price meant to put you off. He is right to. You will find most of yours in the field.
You have four essences and one ability from each. There are ten in each of them and you may claim five. Twenty, in the end.
And a stone wakes one.
A stone wakes one. Not the one you wanted — that is not how it works and everybody asks. Hold it in your off hand and use it.
Bronze is not open to you until all twenty are awake. The Society is not being difficult. It is being honest about what a bronze contract does to somebody who is half made.

society.greeter.notyet.name: Vail — four stars, and not ready

lines.text: Four stars. The work is not the problem — the work has been good.
Then what is?
You are half awake. Twenty abilities in four essences, and you are carrying fewer. Bronze does not care how brave you were at iron.
Stones. Off the things you kill, mostly, and Corvel has them at a price designed to make you go and kill things. Come back when all twenty are open and the seal is already in the drawer.
Vail sent you round. She does that with the ones she thinks will come back.
Everything on the racks is yours if you pay for it. Buy the dagger today and the spear when you have the marks — it reaches a thing before the thing reaches you.
The tour. Right. Bottles, shelf, do not touch.
Red ones close what is open. Carry one in your off hand — a potion in your bag is a potion you did not drink.
Mind the step. Everyone forgets the step.
Rope, oil, salt — and the grey lumps on the middle shelf, which are awakening stones and cost more than you have. Most people find theirs in the field. Come back when you have not.
Then go and look at all three of them before you take anything. It is ten minutes and it will save you an afternoon.
Sella first, on your left going out. Then Ivens opposite. Then Corvel, further up.
Adventurer. I am not a clerk, whatever the desk looks like. I keep the things the clerks decide are not worth keeping.

choices.say: The clay pit came out at twelve.
The thing under Coldbrook said four numbers.
The bells were ringing an order.

lines.text: Wren. Archivist. The Society writes down what a contract paid and what killed the last person who took it, and then it throws away everything in between.
I keep the in between. Nine tenths of it is a waste of a shelf. The other tenth is the reason this province still has people in it.
And you tell adventurers about it because?
Because a pattern nobody is standing inside is a curiosity, and one somebody is standing inside is a warning. Bring me the odd ones. I will tell you what they rhyme with.

choices.say: I will keep an eye out.

lines.text: Then go and be paid for something. Come back when a job has a number in it that will not sit still.

society.wren.1.name: Wren — the line in the ledger

lines.text: You sat with it. Good. What did it write?
One line. Four words and a number, in a hand nobody at the Society writes in.
Say the number.
Eleven.
Eleven. And the four words will have been a place, and the place will have been Lowford, and I would very much like to be wrong about that.
It has written a place and a number four times in ninety years and every time the number came down by one. It is at eleven. Go and look at Lowford.
From fifteen, in the year the Society took this building. Nobody wrote down what happened at zero because it has not happened yet.
That is the entire archive on the subject. Four lines, ninety years, one hand. Go to Lowford.
Halder counted twelve barrows up out of a pit eleven went down into. How many times?
Four days out of the fortnight. Never the same day twice.
Four. It is always four.
And the twelfth barrow?

There is no twelfth barrow. There is a count that has been given one more than it was given, and something in the clay very carefully making the sum come out. It is not hiding. It is showing its working.
To whatever is keeping the tally, and it is not the thing in the pit. The thing in the pit is a nib.
Somebody at Marrowgate wrote to the clerks last month about a book that adds a line. Take that one. I want to know whether the hand is the same.
Well?
Same hand. Same nights. Ninety miles apart and the ink dries at the same hour.
Then it is not a haunting and it is not a hoax, it is a LEDGER, and it is being kept properly, which is very much worse.
Two books, one clerk, and nothing between them but ninety miles of very ordinary road.
What is it counting?
That is the silver question and you are not silver. Get there.

choices.say: Give me something to work with.

lines.text: A count that goes down is not an inventory. It is a notice.
And a notice ninety miles wide, kept in two books for ninety years, in a hand that does not tire, is somebody being extremely polite about something they intend to do.
Say them.
Four. Three. Three. Two.
With gaps.
A day between each. It stopped at two and it has not said anything for nine days.

It has not stopped. It is waiting for the rest of the sum, and the rest of the sum is somewhere else — the bells at Marrowgate have been ringing an order for nine nights and the watch has been writing it down like idiots and calling it a nuisance.
Go and listen to the bells. Bring me the order.
Everything is arithmetic if you are patient enough to be frightened by it. This has been patient for ninety years.
Four, three, three, two. Six bells. Do not tell me what you think it adds up to until you have stood under it.

society.wren.5.name: Wren — the order of the bells

lines.text: Nine nights, six bells, no repeats. And the first four nights were four, three, three, two.
Of course they were.

It is not sending a message to us. It is checking its own working against something that answers, and the thing that answers walks the boundary at Winterbourne on the first clear night of the month and is one person longer every time.
The procession.

The procession is the count made visible, and two of the people in it are known to the diocesan office by name. Break it, or stand in it, or whatever the seal on that contract turns out to say. And come back.
One of them was a silver adventurer who took the Coldbrook contract in the year I came here. The other was the clerk who wrote the second entry in the ledger.
They are both walking, and neither of them is alive, and the office is describing this as a procession.

society.wren.6.name: Wren — what the count is for

lines.text: You stood in it.
For ninety seconds. It went round me.
And it was longer at the end than the beginning, and you were not asked to join it, which is the first useful thing anybody has brought me in nine years.
It is counting DOWN, and it is counting people it has already got. Eleven. Then Lowford. Then the twelfth barrow that was not a barrow.
Eleven what?
Eleven more. And then a page that is full, and a book that is finished, and whatever a thing like that does on the day it has nothing left to write.
There is a gold contract called Close the Ledger. It is one page and you may read it once. I have never been allowed to read it. Take it.

choices.say: My name comes off the roll if I do.

lines.text: Yes. On the day you leave, not the day you come back, which is the Society being careful rather than the Society being cruel.
It has been careful about this for ninety years. That is the part I have never forgiven it for.
Sit down. You are bleeding on a floor I have to look at.
It is closed.
Say the number.
There was no number. The last page was blank and the hand had stopped.
Blank.

Ninety years, two books, eleven to go, and it ends on a blank page because somebody walked in and stood in front of it. I am going to write that down, and the clerks are going to decide it is not worth keeping, and I am going to keep it anyway.
Your name went back on the roll this morning. Nobody will tell you that, so I am.

society.wren.7b.name: Wren — what it was counting to

lines.text: Zero. Everything counts to zero. The question was always what it thought was going to be standing there when it arrived.
Now it is a blank page in a locked room and the answer is: nothing, and you.

society.clerk.silver.what.name: Clerk Vane — what is up here

lines.text: Nothing on this floor is a lump of rock with a temper. That is the first thing and it catches everyone.
Processionals walk in a line and reach four metres, and the flagstones they walk on put them back together. You do not stop one. You are in its way until it has gone past.
Tallymen hit like a cold. Nothing, and nothing, and nothing, for as long as there is ash on the floor — and there is always ash on the floor.
And the third thing?
Glasswrights. Seventy pounds of nothing moving very fast, and if it lands twice you are a sheet in my drawer. Do not let it land twice.

choices.say: Which of them would you take?

lines.text: Two of the five have a Verge in them. You will want to know what that is before you sign, and I would rather tell you than have you read it standing up.
It is the size of a gatehouse. It moves at the speed of grass. And every green thing it is standing on is putting it back together faster than most people can take it apart.
So fight it on stone.
Yes. That is the whole contract, and it has killed four people who also knew that. Knowing it and being able to make it happen are different floors of this building.

choices.say: Are you obliged to say that?
I will read it standing up anyway.
